Both tests are answers to a structural puzzle the privilege wasn't built for: a corporation is a legal fiction that can only speak through people, so *which* people count as "the client"? Every employee is an agent, but treating all of them as the client risks letting a company wrap any inconvenient fact in privilege simply by routing it past a lawyer.

## The control group test

Formulated by Judge Kirkpatrick in *City of Philadelphia v. Westinghouse Electric Corp.*, 210 F. Supp. 483 (E.D. Pa. 1962). His framing question was whether it is really the corporation seeking the lawyer's advice when the communication is made. His answer: if the employee making the communication, whatever his rank, is in a position to control or take a substantial part in a decision the corporation may make on the attorney's advice  or is an authorized member of a body with that authority  then he personifies the corporation and the privilege applies. Everyone else is merely supplying information to enable the lawyer to advise those who do have authority to act. The authority has to be actual, not apparent.

So the privilege tracks decision-making power. Officers, directors, and senior managers are in; a line supervisor or plant technician relaying facts is out, even if the lawyer specifically asked for those facts.

The rationale is that the privilege exists to protect the *client's* candor in seeking advice, and only the decision-makers are meaningfully in that posture. The criticism is that it inverts how corporations actually work. The people who know what happened are usually not the people who decide what to do about it, and the people who create legal exposure are frequently mid- or low-level employees. A rule that protects only the top of the org chart discourages exactly the fact-gathering that lets counsel give sound advice.

This extends the privilege to any employee wh"has information related to the subject matter of his employment that the corporation's attorney needs. A warehouse worker describing a loading procedure is covered if the company is seeking advice about that procedure and he was directed to speak.
